title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit that tested whether conservative, deterministic contamination detectors (exact‑match + fuzzy 5‑gram + provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered contamination controls changes validator‑based success rates. Under preregistration study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 we ran 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) using a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics and a deterministic netops validator. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags; consequently no guarded exclusions/replacements occurred. All 150 baseline episodes and their matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We report artifact‑backed reconciliation between preregistration and execution (SHA references), explain why the outcome is degenerate (synthetic provenance + shared generation semantics), and discuss implications for more sensitive future audits.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level NetOps intent into concrete configuration actions and automated repairs. Reliable operational adoption requires trustworthy evaluation: benchmark contamination (memorized items) and construct invalidity (templated tasks) can inflate measured model success and mislead deployment decisions. Motivated by methodological critiques of LLM evaluation and by recent LLM‑for‑NetOps benchmark/system papers, we preregistered an artifact‑anchored audit asking: After freezing a deterministic contamination‑detection and realism‑adjustment protocol, how many high‑confidence contamination flags occur in a reproducible 150‑item sample, and how much does applying those preregistered controls change the model's validator pass rate? Our primary contributions are (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end under the frozen plan; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) a concise preregistration→execution reconciliation and diagnostics explaining the observed degenerate null and prescribing stronger future audit designs.
sections.related_work: Prior empirical and systems work demonstrates that LLMs can produce plausible network configurations in constrained settings but often introduce regressions unless paired with verification or iterative repair loops; agentic integrations that combine LLMs with validators and iterative validate–repair stages improve average reliability but still admit per‑case failures [arXiv:2604.22513; doi:10.48550/arxiv.2606.06212]. Deterministic/formal network verification tools (header‑space style analyzers, NetKAT/NetPlumber families) are standard oracles for reachability and policy correctness and motivate using formal validators in produce–validate experiments [Kazemian et al.; Beckett et al.]. Survey and meta‑evaluation literature documents contamination and construct‑validity risks in LLM benchmarks and recommends provenance tracing, n‑gram overlap heuristics, and manual adjudication for borderline cases; we operationalize a conservative subset of those recommendations in a preregistered design [evaluation surveys]. This audit is methodological: it assesses preregistered detectors and treatment rules under a reproducible sample and reporting regime rather than proposing new LLM architectures or production claims.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand — We froze the plan in preregistration study contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference guarded_minus_baseline tested by a paired McNemar test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration artifact SHA‑256 is 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a. Sampling and generation semantics — The preregistration allowed deterministic replacement of excluded items and prespecified a confirmatory sample size of 150 item pairs (task_count = 150; planned_episode_count = 300). The executed run used a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) that produced provenance‑normalized synthetic items; executed task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55. To reduce model‑call variance the preregistration specified shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) and the execution honored that choice. Contamination detectors and guarded treatment — Preregistered detectors: (1) exact normalized token equality, (2) fuzzy 5‑gram overlap (5‑gram shingle overlap/Jaccard) with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80, and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics vs model cutoff. Guarded treatment excluded only high‑confidence flagged items and deterministically replaced them with retemplated + topology‑augmented items sampled from the same generator distribution. Validator and model configuration — The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and the episode pass/fail oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Analysis plan and artifacts — The confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1; the archived analysis input/results artifact SHA‑256 = 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586. Key preregistered vs executed values (preregistration→execution reconciliation): preregistration SHA = 9a5e11c5... (preregistration artifact); planned_episode_count = 300 (preregistration) → completed_episode_count = 300 (execution manifest); maximum_model_calls planned = 300 → model_calls_used = 150 (execution: shared_initial generation per item); independent_condition_generation planned = false → executed = false; sample provenance planned = allowed deterministic replacements from listed benchmark_scope → executed sample source_identifier prefix = "synthetic-netops:" (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA above). Contamination summary artifact: analysis/contamination_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222. Paired contingency artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e.
sections.results: Execution accounting — planned episodes 300 (150 items × 2 conditions); completed episodes 300; model_calls_used 150 (shared initial generation per item); maximum_model_calls 300; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 150 (deterministic reconciliation). Contamination detection — preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags for the executed sample (analysis/contamination_summary.csv; SHA‑256 389227f0...). Scoring outcomes — baseline_success_count = 150/150 (success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 150/150 (success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency — n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 c2ba9cdb...). Primary inference — paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (analysis/results.json; analysis artifacts referenced above; analysis input SHA = 5337998d1d...). Representative per‑episode validator traces and raw responses are archived (representative examples appear in the execution evidence bundle). No episodes failed, no exclusions/replacements were applied (complete_pair_count = 150).
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the degenerate null — All 150 paired observations were concordant passes (n11 = 150); there were no discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0). Under this degeneracy the McNemar test and paired bootstrap are numerically precise but inferentially vacuous (p = 1.0; CI collapsed), because no observed disagreements exist to attribute to the guarded intervention. Artifact‑backed causes — two nonexclusive, artifact‑supported causes explain the degenerate result: (1) the executed sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated deterministically (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599...; source_identifier values use prefix "synthetic-netops:"), so the preregistered high‑confidence heuristics found no exact or high fuzzy overlaps; and (2) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) produced identical model outputs across baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred, eliminating sensitivity to generation‑level interventions. Power and detectable‑effect considerations — the preregistration included sensitivity curves and planning notes: detecting a 5 percentage‑point absolute decrease with 80% power required a substantially larger paired design (the preregistration documents that ~600 pairs were the multi‑model planning benchmark and that single‑model plans of 300 or fewer pairs increase the minimal detectable effect). The executed Npairs = 150 therefore lacked the preregistered power to reliably detect small (≈5 pp) effects; the preregistration sensitivity artifacts are archived under the preregistration SHA above (9a5e11c5...). Practical implications and recommendations — this run provides evidence that, under (i) conservative deterministic detectors, (ii) provenance‑stable synthetic sampling, and (iii) shared generation semantics, the guarded exclusion policy did not change validator outcomes. It does not imply absence of contamination in public web‑sourced benchmarks, in other LLMs, under independent condition generation, or when using richer/paraphrase‑sensitive detectors plus human adjudication. For more sensitive future audits we recommend: provenance‑rich sampling from web sources, independent generation across conditions, multi‑model scope, layered fuzzy/paraphrase detectors with human adjudication for borderline flags, and explicit power calculations matching the targeted minimal detectable effect.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The null outcome is artifact‑backed and arises from the executed sample composition (deterministic synthetic items) and the preregistered shared‑generation semantics; it does not generalize to public, web‑sourced benchmarks, other detectors, or other models. We provide explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation (SHAs and counts), correct an analysis identifier mapping between preregistered and archived analysis records, and recommend stronger audit designs to increase sensitivity to contamination and construct‑validity issues.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
